title: ConvergeStop: Inference-Time Convergence-Based Halting for Generative Text Embeddings

raw.stage1:
### Purpose
The contribution's purpose is to reduce the computational cost of generative text embeddings that use a fixed number of refinement iterations. Paper [1] introduces GIRCSE, which uses iterative refinement for generative text embeddings, but does not explicitly aim to reduce computational cost. Paper [17] compares fixed and adaptive computation time for recurrent neural networks, which aligns with the goal of reducing computational cost by adapting computation. Paper [18] introduces Adaptive Computation Time (ACT), which allows RNNs to dynamically adjust the number of computational steps, directly targeting computational efficiency. Both [17] and [18] share the same objective of reducing computational cost in iterative processes, making the purpose covered.

### Mechanism
The mechanism, ConvergeStop, halts refinement iterations when the cosine similarity between consecutive embeddings exceeds a threshold for a fixed number of steps. Paper [4] discusses early stopping criteria before convergence, but it focuses on training rather than inference. Paper [6] proposes a gradient-based early stopping criterion, but it is specific to training optimization. Paper [9] introduces a stopping criterion for the mean shift iterative algorithm, which halts based on entropy thresholds, conceptually similar to halting based on a convergence metric. Paper [10] proposes instance-dependent early stopping, which halts training based on individual learning statuses, but does not use cosine similarity or embedding convergence. Paper [11] introduces a stopping criterion for iterative decoding, which halts based on iterative numbers and SNRs, but does not track embedding convergence. None of these papers use the same mechanism of cosine similarity-based halting for embeddings, making the mechanism uncovered.

### Evaluation
The evaluation design involves measuring compute reduction and retrieval quality on SciFact and FiQA2018 datasets. Paper [1] evaluates generative text embeddings using iterative refinement on retrieval tasks, which matches the benchmark family and metric semantics (e.g., nDCG@10). Paper [5] evaluates iterative refinement sentence embeddings on SciTail, which is a similar retrieval task with comparable metrics. Paper [3] evaluates embedding refinement for text-video retrieval, which shares the same benchmark family and metric semantics. These prior papers use the same evaluation design (retrieval tasks with nDCG metrics), making the evaluation covered.

### Domain
The domain is text embedding retrieval. Paper [1] explicitly operates in the domain of generative text embeddings for retrieval tasks. Paper [5] also works on sentence embeddings for retrieval tasks. Paper [13] improves word embeddings through iterative refinement, which is closely related to text embedding retrieval. Paper [3] applies embedding refinement to text-video retrieval, which is cross-modal but still falls within the broader domain of embedding-based retrieval. These papers address the same general application area, making the domain covered.

**PURPOSE: Cut computational cost of generative text embeddings that use a fixed number of refinement iterations (e.g., GIRCSE's K=20).**

Paper [1] introduces GIRCSE with fixed K=20 iterations but does not address cutting its computational cost — it introduces the system, not optimizes it. Papers [18] and [21]/[22]/[27] address reducing computation in RNNs/DNNs via adaptive halting, but their purpose is reducing inference cost in classification/sequence models, not in generative text embedding refinement loops. No prior paper has the specific purpose of reducing the fixed-iteration cost of generative text embedding refinement. The closest is the general "reduce fixed-iteration compute" objective, which appears in early-exit and ACT literature ([18], [21], [22], [27]), but those target classification networks, not iterative embedding refinement. At the problem-class level, the purpose "eliminate wasted compute from fixed iteration budgets by halting early" is shared with [18] (ACT for RNNs) and [27] (early-exit DNNs survey). Paper [18] explicitly states "allows recurrent neural networks to learn how many computational steps to take" — same objective of replacing fixed iterations with adaptive halting to save compute.

**MECHANISM: ConvergeStop — training-free inference-time halting rule tracking running-mean embedding, halting when cosine similarity between consecutive intermediate embeddings exceeds threshold τ for M consecutive steps.**

This is a cosine-similarity-based convergence detection on intermediate representations, applied at inference time without training. Paper [9] proposes "a new stopping criterion for the mean shift iterative algorithm" using entropy-based thresholds — similar spirit but different signal. Paper [18] (ACT) learns halting probabilities during training — requires training, not training-free. Papers [21]/[22]/[27] use confidence scores at exit branches — require trained classifiers. The specific primitive of "monitor cosine similarity between consecutive intermediate embeddings, halt when it exceeds τ for M consecutive steps using a running mean" is a convergence-detection heuristic. Paper [9] uses a stopping criterion based on comparing consecutive states of an iterative algorithm (entropy of consecutive iterations), which is structurally equivalent: monitor a similarity/change metric between consecutive iteration outputs, halt when below threshold. This is the same primitive — "halt iterative algorithm when consecutive outputs are sufficiently similar" — just using entropy vs. cosine similarity. Paper [4] ("Before Convergence Early Stopping Criterion") also appears relevant but has minimal content shown. The running-mean aspect adds slight nuance, but the core primitive of cosine/similarity-based convergence detection between consecutive iterates appears in [9].

**EVALUATION: nDCG@10 on SciFact and FiQA2018 benchmarks, comparing compute-matched baselines and full-refinement quality.**

The evaluation uses BEIR benchmark datasets (SciFact, FiQA2018) with nDCG@10, a standard IR evaluation metric. Paper [1] (GIRCSE) evaluates on BEIR benchmarks with nDCG@10. This is the same benchmark family and metric. The compute-matched comparison is a standard ablation/substitution design. The evaluation design (BEIR + nDCG@10) is covered by [1].

**DOMAIN: Text embedding retrieval.**

Paper [1] explicitly operates in text embedding retrieval. Paper [3] (MERLIN) operates in text-video retrieval. Paper [5] operates in sentence embeddings for NLI. Paper [13] operates in word embeddings. Paper [1] directly covers text embedding retrieval.

No prior paper explicitly validates the premise that embedding stability during generation is a usable halting signal. While papers like [18] and [21] discuss stability-based stopping criteria, they focus on active learning or error stability, not embedding stability as a halting signal. Similarly, [29] addresses halting problems but in the context of quantum computation, not embedding generation. None of the prior papers establish the same empirical relationship between embedding stability and halting.

### Mechanism
The mechanism involves analyzing cosine-similarity stability of intermediate embeddings across refinement steps and its relation to retrieval ranking. Paper [5] studies cosine-similarity in embeddings, but its focus is on whether cosine-similarity reflects semantic similarity, not stability across refinement steps. Paper [6] discusses iterative refinement algorithms, but it does not analyze embedding stability or its relation to retrieval ranking. Paper [17] introduces iterative refinement for embeddings but focuses on generative text embeddings optimized under contrastive objectives, not stability analysis. None of the prior papers use the same mechanism.

Paper [13] evaluates embedding stability but focuses on sensitivity to training corpus variations, not monotonic stability across refinement steps or its predictive relationship to retrieval ranking. Paper [19] uses cosine-similarity for incremental clustering but does not evaluate monotonic stability or retrieval-ranking prediction. No prior paper uses the same evaluation design.

The domain is text embedding retrieval. Papers [5], [13], and [19] all operate in the general area of text embedding retrieval, even though their specific focus differs (e.g., cosine-similarity analysis, embedding stability under corpus changes, or incremental clustering).
